fixes.explanation: Right, friend. David says “…all people will come to You.” (Psalm 65:2) He doesn't limit it to Zion. He calls God the One who listens to prayer, and he says all people will come to Him.

David doesn't say that here, friend. He says “…You atone for our transgressions.” (Psalm 65:3) To atone is to make things right for a wrong, so the verse is about God dealing with the transgressions. It says nothing about God keeping a record of them.

David doesn't say that here, friend. He says, “We are filled with the goodness of Your house, the holiness of Your temple.” (Psalm 65:4) Goodness is the one he names first, not weight. He says they're filled, and what fills them is good.

That's right. David says, “You stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves…” (Psalm 65:7) Stilled is the word he uses for what God did. The roaring and the pounding are the very things he says God stilled.

That's not the word David uses, friend. He says, “You stilled the roaring of the seas, the pounding of their waves…” (Psalm 65:7) The word is stilled, not divided. The roaring and the pounding are what God stilled.

That's not what David says, friend. He says, “Those who live far away fear Your wonders…” (Psalm 65:8) Mocking would treat the wonders like a joke, and fear takes them seriously. The people far away are the ones who fear.
David doesn't say that, friend. He says, “Those who live far away fear Your wonders…” (Psalm 65:8) Forgetting isn't in the verse. What he says about the faraway people is that they fear.

David doesn't say that here, friend. He says, “You attend to the earth and water it; with abundance You enrich it.” (Psalm 65:9) Measuring and dividing are about carving up land, but this verse is about God caring for the earth. He waters it and enriches it with abundance.

Storehouses aren't in this verse, friend. David says, “…You prepare our grain by providing for the earth.” (Psalm 65:9) The word is our, and what God prepares is grain. It's the grain itself, not a building to put it in.
Yes, friend. David says, “You soften it with showers and bless its growth.” (Psalm 65:10) Showers are what soften the ground. God also blesses its growth.

David doesn't say hail, friend. He says, “You soften it with showers and bless its growth.” (Psalm 65:10) Hail would beat on the ground, but showers soften it. God is blessing the growth here, not battering it.
Frost isn't in this verse, friend. David says, “You soften it with showers and bless its growth.” (Psalm 65:10) Showers do the softening. God also blesses its growth.

True, friend. David says, “You crown the year with Your bounty, and Your paths overflow with plenty.” (Psalm 65:11) The year gets a crown, and the crown is God's bounty. His paths overflow with plenty too.
That's it, friend. David says, “The pastures are clothed with flocks, and the valleys are decked with grain.” (Psalm 65:13) The pastures are clothed with flocks. The valleys are decked with grain.
Yes, friend. David ends with, “They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing.” (Psalm 65:13) The pastures and valleys are the ones shouting and singing. The song closes on that sound.
David doesn't say that, friend. He says, “They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing.” (Psalm 65:13) The words are shout and sing, not rest and wait. Resting and waiting aren't in the verse.
